newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian commercial banks flocking to Japan.
newsitem.headline: Asian commercial banks flocking to Japan.

text.p: Asian commercial banks, full of vigour as a result of robust economic growth in their countries, are spreading their wings and expanding to Tokyo, bankers say.
This is in sharp contrast to the tendency in the past few years among some American and European banks in Tokyo to reduce or halt their operations in Japan.

Commercial banks from China, Taiwan, South Korea and the Philippines have opened branch offices in Japan over the last two years, compared with only one bank from Europe and the United States combined, the Finance Ministry said.

An official for the Institute of Foreign Bankers (IFB), a foreign bankers" body in Japan, said the recent rush of Asian banks into Japan is mainly due to the growth of Asian banks and the development of financial systems in their countries.

"It (the influx of Asian banks into Japan) is probably a reflection not necessarily of Japan as a great big magnet, but the fact that banks in countries such as the Philippines are better banks...than they were 10 years ago," the IFB official said.

The Asian banks which have set up branch offices in Japan over the last two years are Korea"s Housing and Commercial Bank, Korea Long-Term Credit Bank, Bank of Taiwan, China's Bank of Communications, the Philippine National Bank (PNB) and Metropolitan Bank & Trust Co (Metrobank).
The Manila-based Asian Development Bank (ADB) also set up a representative office in Tokyo late last year.
In the case of Philippine banks, deregulation of Manila"s financial markets paved the way for their entry into Japan, bank officials said.

Moriji Matsuda, assistant to the general manager at Metrobank's Tokyo branch, said Philippine banks were apparently able to gain a foothold in Japan as a result of a tacit agreement between Japanese and Philippine authorities.

Metrobank and PNB were granted licences to operate as full branches in Japan in exchange for allowing Fuji Bank and Bank of Tokyo (now Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi ) to enter the Philippines, Matsuda said.
The IFB official said it is only natural for sophisticated Asian banks to come to Japan because of the significant trade ties between Japan and other Asian countries.
Japan's trade with the rest of Asia totalled 33.478 trillion yen ($269 billion) in 1996, accounting for about 40 percent of Japan"s entire trade volume, MOF said.
Meanwhile, the number of European and North American banks in Japan has decreased, as some scaled back operations due to changes in strategy, the IFB official said.
"Banks...in most developed countries have become more stringent about profitability targets...They don"t see as much of a need to be in a place just to have a flag there," the official said.

Isabelita Manalastas, vice president and managing director of PNB's Tokyo branch, said that trade finance is a promising source of business for Philippine banks in Japan, especially as the Philippines has become a popular destination for Japanese investment in recent years.

The Japanese were the most active foreign investors in Philippine economic zones in 1996, with investments amounting to 12.297 billion pesos ($467 million), data from the Philippine Economic Zone Authority showed.
Japan, despite its high costs, is attractive in other ways as well, PNB's Manalastas said.

One of the areas which PNB is concentrating on is remittances to the Philippines by Filipinos in Japan, Manalastas said. Officials for PNB and Metrobank said they estimate that about 100,000 to 150,000 Filipinos now live in Japan. ($=124 yen) ($=26.3 pesos)
